title: Texas payrolls lose 18,900 jobs while more firms report raising prices
summary: September’s payroll decline interrupted an already slow quarter for Texas. The state lost 18,900 jobs during the month, a seasonally adjusted 1.6% annualized contraction. Over the third quarter as a whole employment still rose at a 0.2% annualized pace. Growth from December through September was 0.8% annualized. The Dallas Fed lowered its 2026 Texas employment growth forecast to 0.9% following the September report. These are four different measures of momentum, and the 18,900 figure is the actual monthly change in the payroll count.

The sector chart makes the aggregate slowdown easier to interpret. Third-quarter employment grew at a 3.8% annualized rate in manufacturing and 2.4% in professional and business services. Professional and business services represented 15.0% of state payrolls, against 6.9% for manufacturing, so a ranking by sector growth alone misses the relative scale of their contributions. Construction swung from 2.4% growth over the first nine months to a 3.1% contraction in the quarter. Trade, transportation and utilities, the largest grouping at 19.3% of payrolls, contracted 0.3% in the quarter. Oil and gas employment grew 0.9% in the quarter but represented only 1.4% of jobs. Strong energy exports could therefore coexist with soft aggregate hiring.

The separate unemployment measure held at 4.4%, compared with 4.2% nationally. The state labor force grew at a 1.2% annualized pace in September and was nearly flat against a year earlier. Wage growth also remained stronger than the headline employment figure might suggest. Texas private hourly earnings averaged $36.34 over three months, below the national $37.74, yet the year-over-year increase in the smoothed series was 5.3% in Texas against 3.1% nationally. The state can close part of a wage-level gap while still paying less per hour. The earnings average does not establish how much any individual worker’s pay rose.

The price indicators refer to different months. August headline Texas CPI rose 2.2% from a year earlier, while core CPI rose 3.1%. Energy prices rose 16.6% and housing prices 1.4%. In the October business surveys, the manufacturing prices-received index rose to 29.9 against a series average of 9.3. The services selling-price index reached 18.2 against an average of 7.5. These diffusion readings describe the breadth of reported price changes. They cannot be entered as percentage rates of consumer inflation or assumed to pass through immediately to the August basket.

Real, seasonally adjusted exports rose 6.5% in August and 20.3% from a year earlier. Oil and gas, 29.5% of the export mix shown in the chart, rose 14.9% on the month. Petroleum and coal products, computers and electronics, and chemicals also rose, while transportation equipment fell 4.1%. The release suggests that the Iran war likely contributed to elevated oil and gas activity. Its export series documents the concentration and timing of the increase, but provides no decomposition of that proposed mechanism.

questions.question: Which industries account for the weakness extending beyond September?
questions.detail: Use the chart’s sector weights and changes in employment levels to quantify contributions. Compare September with the quarter and the first nine months, with particular attention to construction and the large trade, transportation and utilities grouping. The payroll release warns that earlier observations can be revised, so retain the series as published here when testing what was knowable in November.

questions.question: Do the October selling-price reports precede broader consumer inflation?
questions.detail: Track the manufacturing and services diffusion indexes against subsequent monthly consumer prices in closely related categories. Keep the August 12-month CPI readings separate from the October survey balances. An increase in the share of firms raising prices gives limited information about individual price changes or how quickly buyers will face them.

questions.question: Did export growth translate into stronger demand for Texas labor?
questions.detail: Compare real export categories and payroll industries on aligned months, using the distinction between oil and gas’s 29.5% share of exports and its 1.4% share of jobs. The release’s sector series make concentration visible. Establishing an employment response would require additional observations after August and allowances for other goods-producing sectors.

limitation: This November release combines August prices and trade, September labor data and October surveys. Its six charts use different units and reference periods, and the publisher flags possible revisions.
